summaries.example: Imagine choosing a snack after school. In theory, you could learn every snack’s price, taste, and health information, then calculate the perfect choice. In real life, you have limited time and information. You might choose the first snack that looks good enough. That can be a sensible choice when searching longer would take too much effort.
summaries.summary: Bounded rationality is the study of how agents make effective choices when they cannot know everything or calculate everything. An ideal economic model imagines a person with complete information, perfect foresight, and unlimited ability to find the best option. Herbert Simon argued that this picture leaves out the limits faced by real people and other organisms. People often use simple rules, stop when they find something acceptable, or depend on useful features of their surroundings. A decision can therefore be reasonable even when it is not the mathematically best choice under ideal conditions. The entry also explains that there is no single meaning of “rational.” A choice might be judged by its logical consistency, its accuracy, its success in the world, or the effort needed to make it.
key_ideas: Perfect decision-making is an ideal model, but real people have limited information, time, memory, and computing ability.
A simple choice can be sensible if finding the very best choice would cost too much effort.
Satisficing means stopping when an option is good enough instead of searching forever.
A rule may work well in one setting and poorly in another. The surroundings matter.
People disagree about whether a shortcut is a mistake or a useful tool that fits the situation.
summaries.why_it_matters: This idea helps us understand everyday choices without quickly calling people foolish. It also matters for designing schools, workplaces, computer programs, and rules. A method that uses less time or information may work better in a real situation than a complicated method that is difficult to use. To judge a decision fairly, we should ask what information, time, memory, and tools were actually available.

important_terms.definition: Making a good choice while working with limits on time, information, memory, or thinking power.
A made-up model of a person who knows every option and consequence and can calculate the best choice perfectly.
A shortcut or simple rule used to make a judgment or choice.
Choosing the first option that reaches a level you think is good enough.
A rule saying that people should choose the option with the greatest expected benefit, using probabilities.

questions_to_think_about: When is choosing a good-enough option wiser than searching for the absolute best one?
Can a shortcut be helpful in one situation but unhelpful in another?
What information would you need before calling a choice rational?
Should we judge a decision only by its result, or also by the time and effort it took?

summaries.example: Suppose a student is choosing a college course. A perfect optimizer would compare every possible course, predict every consequence, and calculate which maximizes personal utility. A boundedly rational student may set an aspiration level—such as acceptable workload, interest, and schedule—then stop searching after finding a course that meets those requirements. Whether this is a good strategy depends on the student’s goals, the cost of further search, and the structure of the available information.
summaries.summary: Bounded rationality concerns models of judgment and decision-making that depart from the perfect rationality associated with homo economicus. The ideal agent has complete information, perfect foresight, and enough computational power to maximize utility. Expected utility theory formalizes this ideal through axioms governing preferences over prospects: ordering, the Archimedean condition, and independence. Altering these axioms can represent incomplete preferences, lexicographic priorities, or departures from linear probability weighting, although such alterations are not all bounded-rationality theories. The central contribution of bounded rationality is to take seriously the procedures by which decisions are made and the environments in which they occur. Procedural rationality compares accuracy with effort and supports strategies such as satisficing. Ecological rationality studies how cognitive strategies match environmental structure. The entry also separates descriptive, prescriptive, and normative inquiry, and emphasizes that “rationality” may mean coherence, accuracy, successful adaptation, or something else. Consequently, judging a decision requires specifying the object of evaluation, the standard, and the relevant constraints.
key_ideas: The ideal of global rationality differs from the procedures real agents can execute. Limited computation, information, and time are not side issues but central features of decision-making.

Expected utility theory derives a numerical representation of preferences from axioms. Bounded-rationality approaches may weaken ordering, Archimedean, or independence assumptions, but not every departure is automatically a model of bounded rationality.
Procedural rationality evaluates the trade-off between decision quality and the effort required to obtain it. Satisficing is a prominent example.
Ecological rationality evaluates a strategy in relation to environmental structure. A shortcut can be inaccurate by an abstract standard yet effective in a particular setting.

The two major heuristics traditions disagree about normative standards: the biases-and-heuristics program often treats departures from probability or logic as errors, while the fast-and-frugal program asks when a biased rule performs well.
Descriptions of what people do, prescriptions about what they ought to do, and normative standards for evaluation are distinct questions.
summaries.why_it_matters: The framework changes how we assess human judgment, algorithms, and institutions. A model that is optimal without resource limits may be unusable when computation, memory, or information is costly. Conversely, a simple heuristic may outperform a more complex model on new data when the sample is small or the environment has helpful regularities. Bounded rationality therefore does not simply excuse mistakes; it asks which standards and constraints are relevant, how a procedure works, and whether its performance fits the setting.

important_terms.definition: A family of accounts describing, recommending, or evaluating effective behavior when agents have limited information or computational resources.
The idealized economic agent assumed to possess complete information, perfect foresight, and the ability to solve the optimization problem needed to maximize personal utility.
A theory in which preferences over probability-based prospects satisfy ordering, Archimedean, and independence conditions and can therefore be represented by expected utility.
A condition requiring preferences to be complete and transitive: options can be compared, and preference chains do not reverse.
A condition requiring intermediate mixtures of better and worse prospects to be comparable in a continuous way; dropping it permits lexicographic preferences.
A condition requiring that adding the same possible outcome to two prospects preserves their preference ordering; it supports linearity in probabilities.
A decision strategy that searches until it finds an option meeting a predefined aspiration level rather than maximizing across all options.
A simple decision rule whose usefulness depends on how its structural bias fits the environment; it may ignore information yet improve prediction.

questions_to_think_about: If a heuristic predicts accurately but violates a formal axiom, is it irrational, effective, or both under different standards?
When does the cost of computation justify accepting a less accurate or less complete method?
Does dropping completeness represent indecision, ignorance, or a legitimate form of preference?
How should an experiment distinguish a reasoning error from a difference in how participants understood the task?
Can a decision rule be adapted to an environment without being consciously calculated by the agent?

summaries.example: You are buying a used bike. One strategy is to inspect every bike, compare every feature, and calculate the best deal. Another is to decide on a minimum standard—safe brakes, a comfortable size, and a price you can afford—and stop when you find a bike that meets it. The second strategy may miss the absolute best bike, but it saves time. If the seller’s description is unreliable, however, the same shortcut may work badly.
summaries.summary: Bounded rationality is a broad approach to judgment and decision-making under real limits. The idealized homo economicus has complete information, perfect knowledge of consequences, and the computational power to maximize personal utility. Expected utility theory gives this ideal a formal structure: preferences over probability-based prospects can be represented numerically when they satisfy ordering, Archimedean, and independence conditions. Bounded-rationality research asks what happens when these assumptions are weakened or when agents cannot actually perform the required calculations. Simon’s idea of procedural rationality focuses on the trade-off between accuracy and effort, while satisficing describes stopping at an option that is good enough. Ecological rationality adds the structure of the environment: a rule may be successful because it fits the cues and regularities of a particular setting. The entry also describes debates over heuristics. One research tradition emphasizes systematic departures from formal standards; another studies when biased, fast, and simple rules are adaptive. These debates cannot be settled without saying what “rational” means and what standard is being used.
key_ideas: Traditional economic models often describe an agent as if the agent can optimize with complete information and unlimited calculation.
Real decision-makers must balance the quality of a choice against the time and mental effort needed to make it.
Some theories allow incomplete preferences, so a person need not always rank every pair of options.
People may respond differently to gains and losses, and this motivates alternatives to the independence requirement of expected utility theory.
A strategy should be judged in relation to its environment. A shortcut that ignores information can sometimes improve prediction.
The entry distinguishes describing actual behavior, recommending behavior, and choosing the standards used to evaluate behavior.
summaries.why_it_matters: Bounded rationality gives us a more realistic way to think about decisions by people, animals, and machines. It explains why a complex calculation is not always the best practical method and why a simple rule can sometimes perform surprisingly well. It also warns us not to label behavior as irrational before checking the agent’s goals, available information, costs of thinking, and environment. The approach is useful whenever decisions must be made under uncertainty and limited resources.

important_terms.definition: Making judgments or decisions effectively even though an agent has limited information, time, memory, or ability to calculate.
An idealized “economic person” who knows the available options and their consequences and can choose the option with the greatest personal utility.
A mathematical approach that says rational choices among risky prospects maximize expected utility when certain preference rules hold.
A rule that choices should be comparable and should follow consistent chains: if A is preferred to B and B to C, A should be preferred to C.
A rule that prevents infinitely large jumps in preference and supports smooth comparisons between better and worse prospects.
A rule that says adding the same risk or outcome to two choices should not reverse which one is preferred.
A strategy of selecting the first option that reaches a personally acceptable standard.
A simple rule of thumb for making a judgment or decision; its success can depend on the environment.

questions_to_think_about: Would you rather make a fast decision that is usually good or a slow decision that might be perfect?
Can refusing to compare two options be a rational response to missing information?
Why might the same shortcut succeed in one environment and fail in another?
Should a decision be judged by its outcome, its method, or both?
What could researchers learn by studying how people make choices outside a laboratory?
